Introduction: 'quæ Dei furore in rserunt' is damaged; read here as a verb of perishing (e.g. interierunt); 'arserunt' ('burned') is also possible. 'Primo duce' read as 'Primo dice'. 'vident principium Patri' is corrupt, rendered as if 'et inde principium Patri'. 'Ex Pulre Filium, et Spiritu sancto facta omnia' is probably corrupt (perhaps 'ex Patre per Filium in Spiritu sancto'); rendered literally. Ch. 1: the sentence 'Quia vero non solum unum sunt... subter habes demonstratum' is obscure and perhaps corrupt. Ch. 3: 'item ludi' read as 'item audi'. The citations 'psalm. XXVII' (Ps. 17/18) and 'Joan. XVII' (actually Matt. 4:11) are as printed; the translation gives Ps. 17. Ch. 4: 'Dominum gloria' read as 'gloriae'.

Ch. IX opening: 'vi. dent principium' is obscure; read as 'videant/vident principium' and rendered 'they posit a beginning'. Ch. IX: 'Sed quia dixit Filius' is awkward and possibly corrupt. Ch. X: 'ministraret' read as 'monstraret' (show). Ch. VI: the quotation cited as 'Psalm 20' is Psalm 90 (91):10; Isaiah quotation is Isa. 40:28. Ch. VII: 'rech' read as 'fecit'. Ch. V: Jeremiah quotation is Baruch 3:25, 3:36-38.

Evident scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. Pelio = Petro, accidit = occidit, in formationem = ad informationem, numeramur = numeratur, segregat apostolo = segregat apostolos). Ch. XIV: the list of the fruit of the Spirit is from Galatians 5, though the edition's reference says 1 John 4. 'Spiritus sanctus mihi Sapientia, id est in Christo' looks garbled (cf. Wisdom 7:22, 'in her is a holy spirit of understanding'); translated as it stands. 'cajus cst ipsa caritas' read as 'whose [fruit] love itself is'. Ch. XV: 'Numerus siquidem ordinem sufficit, aequalitas non amittit' appears corrupt; translated as if 'ordinem facit, aequalitas non admittit'. 'sicut Pater Filium' is elliptical; '[begot]' supplied. 'Neque enim locutus est ubi non sit' is obscure in context.

Ch. XIX, last sentence: the Latin is garbled ("aut Filius a Spiritu sancto priori loco a Patre taxatum"); the rendering gives the evident sense. Ch. XX: "[professus]" is an alternative reading printed by the edition. "Spiritus sanctus etiam Filius" (twice) seems corrupt; the quoted verse (Wis. 11:21) speaks of the Spirit of God's power, and the heading probably meant that the Holy Spirit is also [the power of God], like the Son. "Psalm 117" is an error: the verse quoted is Wisdom 9:17. "Psalm XI VIr" is read as 147 (Ps. 146:5 Vulgate). "intrerat" is read as "praeerat" (the presiding official); the closing narrative is somewhat obscure. Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. raritatis = veritatis, Iri = Dei, luis = tuis).

nodes.text: CEREALIS THE BISHOP'S SHORT BOOK AGAINST MAXIMINUS THE ARIAN.
INTRODUCTION.

When Cerealis, bishop of Castellum of the holy catholic faith, came to Carthage, his arrival reached the royal ears, because he was nearer to those cities which have perished by the wrath of God. And when those who had been charged with it asked him whether what rumour had spread abroad was true, and he was recounting it in order, Maximinus, bishop of the Ariomaniacs, came upon them and said to Bishop Cerealis: "Do you see what your sins are doing? That is why God has abandoned you." CEREALIS: "Why has he abandoned us, and not rather you, who slaughter souls under the pen of the Christian name, and do not hold the true faith?" MAXIMINUS: "If you hold the true faith, I will put to you questions on your faith, so that, if you have the true faith, I want you to bring two or three testimonies to settle each single proposition." CEREALIS: "Not two or three, but I will bring many testimonies." MAXIMINUS: "Say first: That the Son is equal to the Father. On unity: that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. How the Father sent the Son. How the Father glorifies the Son. That the Son is almighty. Why the Son said: The Father is greater than I. Or why it was said that the Father handed over the Son. On the free power of the Son. Against what they say: He who begets is the author, [and] so the beginning [belongs] to the Father, etc. Against what they say: that the Father commanded the Son to make creation. That the Holy Spirit is God. That the Holy Spirit is creator. That the Holy Spirit is life-giver. That he too is of his own power and will, and almighty. On the Trinity or unity. That the Son is invisible. Against what they say: That from the Father [came] the Son, and by the Holy Spirit all things were made. Against what they say: Why the Father is named first, then the Son. Against what they say: That the Father subjected all things to him."
THE SHORT BOOK BEGINS.
CHAPTER ONE.

CEREALIS: That the Son is equal to the Father, the apostle Paul teaches thus, saying: Have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God (Phil. 2). He who is in the form of God the Father cannot be less; he did not seize what he did not have, because he was always in the form of the Father. In the Gospel John says: For this reason the Jews wanted to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God (John 5). Again the Lord himself said: He who sees me sees the Father also. Again in the Gospel: I and the Father are one. Here he said "one" for equality, because those who are one are equal. But he said "are" because the Son is another. Yet the Father and the Son are one. For God is not divided, since the Son himself says: I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. But that the Father and the Son are not one alone, with the Holy Spirit added, you have shown below; "one" pertains to the fellowship of both the Father and the Son, and "one" pertains to the one Lord alone, because [this is] the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Again the Lord himself in the Gospel: All things that the Father has are mine. Again the Son himself in the Gospel says to the Father: All mine are yours, and all yours are mine. And again: He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father. Again in the Gospel: He who hates me hates my Father also. Again in the Epistle of John: He who denies the Son does not have the Father either; but he who confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father. Again in Solomon: He is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of his goodness (Wis. 7). This he says of the Son. Again in the Gospel: As the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself. But where he says "granted", "begot" is understood. Or if the Father granted life afterwards to the Son already begotten, then the begotten Son was without life. And how does he himself say in the Gospel: I am the way, the truth, and the life? Again, to the Hebrews the Apostle speaks thus of the Son: Who, since he is, he says, the brightness of glory and the figure of his substance, and upholds all things by the word of his power (Heb. 1). Does not, then, the brightness of glory and the figure of his substance hold the brightness, that is, the truth? And the figure of God is called the equality of God. Again the apostle Paul, to the Colossians, says of the Son: In him, he says, dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. If all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in Christ, how then is the Son less?
CHAPTER 2.

That the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God is taught thus. The Lord himself says in the law: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God. And the Apostle says: There is no God but one. Again he says: one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4). Again the apostle James says: You believe that God is one; you do well; the demons also believe, and tremble (Jas. 2). The demons tremble at this faith, which they did not want to be true. The Lord himself says: I am God, and there is no other besides me. Again in Psalm 17: Who is God but the Lord, or who is God but our God? And they themselves confess that the Son too is God. Let them show me how he is one, except that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one.
CHAPTER III.

How the Father sent the Son is taught thus: The sending of the Son is the incarnation of the Son. The apostle Paul testifies also who was sent, whether the Son of God or the Son of man, saying: God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4). So he who was made of a woman is the one who was sent, and he was also under the law, as he said; for God established the law. Again the same apostle says of Christ: He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2). When he emptied himself, then he sent himself; for the Son himself also says: I came to seek and to save what was lost. Here he does not say "I was sent", but "I came". For the Holy Spirit also sent him, as is written, as he himself teaches, in the prophet Isaiah: And now, he says, the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit (Isa. 48). Again the Son himself says: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, etc. So the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son, if he who sends is greater, since the Holy Spirit sent the Son of God. God is certainly everywhere, for he says: I fill heaven and earth; and elsewhere he says: Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet. How then is the Son sent? Or how does the Father send, if in heaven and on earth the one God is everywhere? Hear, again, where not only equals are sent by equals, but even greater ones are sent by lesser, as we read that an angel was sent by Tobias, and Christ was sent by Pilate to Herod. Did the angel humble himself because he went where he was sent by Tobias? Or did Christ humble himself, who was sent by Pilate to Herod? Do you want to know that the Son is everywhere, and there is nowhere for him to be sent? Hear what the Son himself says: No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven. For he did not say "who was in heaven", but "who is in heaven", and yet he was speaking on earth; but on earth too he was then man and God. For if God was not on earth, how did the angels minister to him, as it is written: And the devil departed, and angels came and ministered to him (John 17)?
CHAPTER IV.

How the Father glorifies the Son is taught thus. For the Son also glorifies the Father, as is written in the Gospel, the Son himself saying to the Father: I have glorified you on earth. Again the Son himself says: Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you. And the Holy Spirit himself glorifies the Son, for it is written: He will glorify me, because he will receive of mine and will announce it to you. If then the Holy Spirit glorifies the Son, the Holy Spirit is by no means greater than the Son. And the Son himself says in the psalm: The sacrifice of praise will honour me. So the sacrifice of praise is understood as the burnt offering of the passion; in the passion, then, the man is glorified, for God is always glorious. Do you want to know that the Son was not only always glorious, but was and is the God of glory? The apostle Paul says of the Jews: For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. Now therefore he who could die is the one who could be glorified, the man only. For hear what the Son himself says, how he sanctifies himself: In truth, he says, I sanctify myself.
CHAPTER V.

That the Son is almighty is taught thus. In Solomon we read: Your almighty word, O Lord, leaping from your royal thrones, sprang into the midst of the land of destruction (Wisdom 18). So he who holds royal thrones is also king. Again in the Apocalypse: These things says the Son of God, who is and who was, almighty God. In the Gospel: Whatever the Father does, these the Son also does likewise (John 5). Again in the Gospel: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills. In Isaiah the Son says: Behold, I will send my hand upon you, and those who plundered you shall be plundered, and you shall know that I am the Lord almighty, and he who sent me is the Lord almighty.

The prophet Jeremiah says: Great is he, and has no end, lofty and immeasurable is this our God, and there is no other. And so that it may be plain that this is said of Christ, there follows: Afterwards he was seen on earth, and lived among men. Again the Apostle: But we, he says, preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God. Again, he himself, when speaking of the Jews: Whose are the fathers, he says, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.
CHAPTER VI.

Why the Son said: The Father is greater than I, and why it is said that the Father handed over his Son, is taught [here]. It is written in the psalm, the Son saying to the Father: From my mother's womb you are my God (Psalm 21). So from his mother's womb the Father is his God, and therefore the Father is greater. Again the Son himself says in the psalm: O Lord, I am your servant, I am your servant and the son of your handmaid (Psalm 115), that is, of Mary. He is a servant, and therefore the Father is greater. Again: God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me (Psalm 21)? And again: Save me from the mouth of the lion. These things belong to the man; for he himself also says: I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again: no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself, and I take it up again (John 20). In the psalm: I lay down and slept, and I rose again, because the Lord upheld me. And the Apostle, [showing] that the Son handed himself over, speaks thus: Who loved me, he says, and handed himself over for me. Again the Apostle himself: Who loved, he says, his Church, and handed himself over for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word. Again Paul in the Epistle to the Ephesians: As Christ also, he says, loved us and handed himself over for us. Again in the psalm he himself says: To do your will, my God, I willed. He says in the psalm "my God", just as he said above: From my mother's womb you are my God. And yet afterwards it follows, when he said: To do your will, my God, he added "I willed"; because he willed, he did [it]: for he is the one of whom it is said: Whatever he willed, he did. He willed to be born, he willed to die, he willed to suffer all things, both to hunger and to thirst and to be weary, and yet according to the man. For do you want to know what the Son of God is like? Isaiah says: The eternal God, who made the ends of the earth, neither laboured nor hungered, etc.; he says it of the Son, of whom it is said: All things were made through him. For God could suffer nothing evil or toilsome, to whom it is said in Psalm 20: Evils shall not come near you, and the scourge shall not approach your dwelling.
CHAPTER VII.

The Son's free power is taught thus. In the Gospel he says: Father, I will that where I am, these too may be with me (John 17). He did not say "I ask". In the Gospel he did not say to the leper "I ask", but "I will, be clean" (Matthew 8). Again in the Gospel, to Peter, when he asked him that he might walk on the water, Jesus said: Come. He did not ask, but said "Come". Again to the Canaanite woman he said: I was sent only to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel (Matthew 15). The woman was a gentile, yet because he willed it, he granted the favour and healed her daughter, though he had said he was not sent to her. For Christ was destined not for the gentiles but for the Jews; then he said: O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you will. And her daughter was healed from that hour. Why did he grant the favour to her, to whom he had said he was not sent? So you see that he did what he willed, not what another commanded. Again in the psalm it says of Christ: Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps. It did not say "whatever he asked".
CHAPTER VIII.

Against what he says: He who begets is greater, he who is begotten is lesser. These things are known by times, but in Christ, through whom all things were made, there are no times. For he who is known to have been begotten before times is not everlasting from time; just as we read that Adam was begotten by no one, and yet he and his son were both alike and equal, because both were men. Greater and lesser come about through times, because one grows old and the other grows up. But with God there were never times.

For times themselves were made through the Son, and nothing in God is temporal. Take away times, then, and show me a greater and a lesser. How the Son is lesser not only than his Father but also than the angels, the apostle Paul says of him to the Hebrews: Now, I say, we have seen Jesus made a little lower than the angels. Why? It follows: Because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2).
CHAPTER IX.

Against what they say: He who begets is the author, [so that] they posit a beginning. There is no authorship for the Father where there is no will. For the Father begot neither willing nor unwilling, but by nature. For if he begot willingly, then the Son is the very will of the Father, as we read. For he is the Word and power and wisdom; he is also the will of the Father. If at some time the Son was not, at some time the Father was not, because he could not be Father if he had not had a Son. But as the Father is eternal, so the Son too is eternal, of whom it is written: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God (John 1). He is not contained by time, he has no beginning, nor is he enclosed by ages. And in the psalm the Son says to the Father: I am always with you. For if the Son was always with the Father, how is the Father the author, who never existed before [him]? Again it is said of him: Before the mountains came to be, and the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are. If, then, the Son is the will of the Father, let it be told me how the Father is the author, without whom the Son never was, since the Father could not be without will? That he is called Father is said on account of the Son; and he is called God from God. But because the Son said [it], that he is called Son is also said on account of the Father. For "I in the Father, and the Father in me" is not separated, but for that reason God is one. But if the Son is lesser than the Father, why did he say "The Father is in me"? The lesser can never contain the greater.
CHAPTER X.

Reply is made against what they say, that the Father commanded the Son to make the creation. For certainly the Father himself also made it, since it is written: Let us make man in our image and likeness (Genesis 1). Here it is shown that they worked together, so as to show that God is one. Scripture continues: And God made man in his own image and likeness. Having said "let us make man", it did not say "the gods made", but said: God made man in his image and likeness. Again, if the Father did not make the creation, how does the Son say: My Father works until now, and I work? Again, if the Father did not make the creation, how do the apostles say to the Father: You are the Lord, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, who by the mouth of your holy servant David said: Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ (Psalm 2). For truly in this city there gathered together against your holy servant Jesus Christ, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate with the gentiles and all Israel, and they did as your hand and your counsel had foreordained (Acts 4). So those who said: You are the Lord, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, were speaking to the Father about Christ. Read in the Acts of the Apostles, and you will find this statement said to the Father about the Son.
CHAPTER XI.

That the Holy Spirit is God is taught thus. Peter said to the man who had held back part of the price of the farm: Why is it that Satan has filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? And afterwards he added: You have not lied to men, but to God (Acts 5). Again, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that, while Peter was pondering and hesitating over the vision, the Holy Spirit says: See, men are looking for you; get up, go down, and go with them without any doubt, because I have sent them to you. And Peter, coming to Cornelius, said: In truth I know that God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10). For he was sent by the Holy Spirit to a gentile, because the Gospel was not yet being preached to the gentiles, but to the Jews alone. Again in the Gospel: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. Or is he not God who fills God? So it was God in Christ, full of whom he returned from the Jordan. Again the Apostle: Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you? He went on: Glorify God, then, in your body. Again in Solomon: The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world. Again Isaiah the prophet: And the Lord said to me: Go, say to this people: With the ear you will hear, and you will not understand, etc. The one whom Isaiah calls God, the Apostle calls the Holy Spirit. If God is spirit, how is the Holy Spirit not God? If the Holy Spirit is not God, how does the apostle Paul say: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of workings, but one God, who works all things in all, who distributes to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12)? He is the Holy Spirit, of whom the prophet Isaiah says: The Spirit, I say, of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord.
CHAPTER XII.

That the Holy Spirit is also creator is taught thus. In Job we read: It is the divine Spirit who made me. In the psalm: Send forth your spirit, and they will be created (Psalm 103). In the Gospel: Mary was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. To her it had been said: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Matthew 1). In the psalm: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power (Psalm 32). If in the virgin's womb the Holy Spirit made the Son of God, what did he lack of God, that he did not create? In the Gospel: Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God. For to regenerate is more than to create: see, the Holy Spirit regenerates, when in baptism we are reborn through him.
CHAPTER XIII.

That the Spirit is the giver of life is taught thus. The Apostle says: The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3). Again in the Gospel: It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no use at all (John 6). In Ezekiel a command is given to the dry bones of the children of Israel, and it is said through the prophet: I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live. Again the Apostle says: But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you (Romans 8:11). So mortal bodies are given life by the Holy Spirit.
CHAPTER XIV.

That the Holy Spirit is also of his own power and will, and is almighty, is taught thus. The Apostle says: To one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for benefit; to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the gift of healings in the one Spirit, to another the working of cures, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another kinds of tongues; but all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12).

See: one and the same Spirit works as he wills, not things that are commanded him. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: The Spirit breathes where he wills (John 3). In the Acts of the Apostles the Spirit orders Philip to join the eunuch of Queen Candace. Again the Spirit says: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the holy work to which I have called them. See, the Holy Spirit sets apart apostles and calls [them]. Again of the apostles: They were trying to go into Bithynia, and the Holy Spirit did not allow them. See, he commands apostles. Again, in Solomon he says: The Holy Spirit [is] Wisdom to me, that is, in Christ. The Holy Spirit [is] unique, manifold, subtle, unmoved, undefiled, sure, secure, loving the good, all-powerful, foreknowing all things, and one who takes in all intelligible spirits, pure [and] subtle. See what the Holy Spirit is like. Again in the Gospel: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee. Christ walks in the power of the Spirit. Again in the Acts of the Apostles we read that the apostles spoke as utterance was given them. The Spirit gave the apostles [the power] to speak as they did. Again the apostle Paul shows what the Holy Spirit bestows, saying: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control (1 John 4). And we read in John the apostle that God is love. If God is love, what is the Holy Spirit, whose [fruit] love itself is? For so you have it above: that the fruit of the Holy Spirit is love (1 John 4).
CHAPTER XV.

On the Trinity and the divinity of the Word. If there is no Trinity, why was it said: Go, baptise all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit? If there is no unity, why was it said in one name, and not in names? If there is no Trinity, why does the Lord say: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? If there is no unity, why does he say God three times, and not call [them] gods together? If there is no Trinity, why do the Seraphim in Isaiah say in praise: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth (Isaiah 6)? Where they show both the Trinity and the unity, since they say God and not gods. If there is no Trinity, why does the Apostle say: From him, and through him, and in him are all things? Or if there is no Trinity or no unity, why does there follow "to him be glory", and not "to them be glory", if the gods are several? But if some wish to take this as said of the Father, then let them not slander the Son, since as the Father [begot] the Son, so through the Son all things were made. Therefore God is not counted, is not increased, does not lack, because he is not diminished. If the Son is certainly God, he does not admit these things in himself; for he himself says to the devil tempting him: You shall not tempt the Lord your God (Matthew 4). And the apostle Thomas says, as he touched the places of his wounds: My Lord and my God. For the Trinity is inseparable. For he has not spoken where he is not. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are everywhere together, and are not separated by places, because God is not bodily; nor is God counted, because he is not subject to numbers. Our God, therefore, is one. For although there is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, no Christian can speak of three Gods, because the divine nature differs from itself in nothing. For number produces order, [which] equality does not admit; for a second follows the first, and a third is attached to the second. But since grades cannot be formed from equals so as to be ranked beneath one another as in counting, there will therefore be one, because he has no second. For a second holds the rank of a lesser, and the lesser makes an other; an other indicates a later, a later signifies an unequal. Remove distance, and you will have nothing to count. The prophet says: Of his wisdom there is no number. If his wisdom is not counted, how is the Son counted, who is the Wisdom of the Father, as the Apostle says? Why is the Son called second after the Father, when wisdom is not counted, since he is the wisdom of the Father?
CHAPTER XVI.

That the Son is invisible is taught thus: No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal [him]. In the Apostle it is written of Christ: He is the invisible, the firstborn of all creation. Again: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first; but for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Christ Jesus might show all his patience as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life: now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. The Son, then, who came to save sinners, is invisible. If the Son is seen, the Father too is seen, since it is written: Whoever sees me sees the Father also.
CHAPTER XVII.

Against their claim that all things are from the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. Hear [this]: you will find it said that all things were made not only from the Father, but also from the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Apostle speaks thus of the Son to the Ephesians: But doing the truth in love, let us grow in him in all things, who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body [is] joined and fitted together. See, [it is] from the Son. Hear also [that it is] from the Holy Spirit: If anyone has not been born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God. And again it is read in the Gospel: So is everyone who is born from the Spirit.
CHAPTER XVIII.

Against their claim that the Father bears witness to the Son. Christ himself says in the Gospel: I am the one who bears witness about myself. So he testifies about himself. The prophets bore witness to the Son: are the prophets then greater than the Son? The apostles bore witness to the Son: are the apostles then greater than the Son of God? But since I have shown that he bore witness to himself, there will be nothing for our opponents to answer: I am, says the Son, the one who testifies about myself.
CHAPTER XIX.

Against their question: Why is the Father named first, and then the Son? Hear that the Son too is named before the Father. The Apostle says to the Galatians: Not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. Again he says to the Thessalonians: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and gave eternal consolation, etc. See, the Son is named first. Hear that the Holy Spirit too is named in the first place. The Apostle says: One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling; one God, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. See, he named the Spirit first and the Father afterwards. But I say: because we read in Leviticus, in a single sentence, Jacob named in first place, Isaac second, Abraham third, must it therefore be said that Jacob was better than Isaac, or Isaac greater than his father Abraham? For so it is written: And I will remember the covenant of Jacob, says the Lord, and the covenant of Isaac, and the covenant of Abraham. If no prejudice is done to men, why should the order of listing bring prejudice upon God, if perhaps somewhere the Father is listed before the Son, or the Son before the Holy Spirit, or [the Holy Spirit] is listed in a place before the Father?
CHAPTER XX.

Against their claim: The Father subjected all things to him. The Apostle says of the Son to the Corinthians: He must, he says, reign until he puts all his enemies under his feet (1 Cor. 15). And to the Philippians: From where we also await the Lord Jesus Christ, our Saviour, who will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able to subject all things to himself (Phil. 3). Again the Apostle says that the Son will hand over the kingdom to God his Father; for it is written of Christ: When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father. Is the Son then greater than the Father, because he himself will hand over the kingdom to his Father? These are the things I have been able to mention and have picked out for the moment; but many have been left out for the sake of speed, which a reader will be able to find. Let the reader hold only this: that the Lord God is in no way subject to number, in no way separated; for what is least is not God, but what God is, the Son and the Holy Spirit each perfectly is [professed to be]. And this is true perfection, which comparison with another does not make subordinate, and in which nothing remains that could increase. God is spirit, not flesh; he is understanding, not a mass; he is inner light, not matter spread around. Therefore Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not divided, because there is nothing that could be cut so as to be separated; and yet the Father is the Father, the Son is the Son, the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit; and they are nowhere without one another, because he who can be understood as one cannot be separated. They are not massed together, since they are not as if made of bronze; they are not divided, since they are not without one another. This is the true catholic faith, which Christ taught and handed down, which the apostles taught, and which all the holy patriarchs and prophets faithfully sang. With the help of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, I have answered your propositions from the New and the Old Testament; now, on behalf of the catholic faith, which is everywhere, I have put forward other testimonies, to which you must reply. In the book of Wisdom: that just as God's wisdom, which is the Son of God, so also the Holy Spirit knows the counsels of the Father. In the same book: that the Son, through whom all things were made, is almighty. In the same book: that the Holy Spirit [is] also the Son, who is called the power of God. In the same book it is said of the Holy Spirit that he is incorruptible. In the same book: it calls Christ visible according to the form of the lowliness he took on, but according to the form of deity declares him not visible but invisible. For what is seen is recognised as man, what is not seen as God. In the same book it is said that the Son of God is of the substance of the Father. In the Song of Songs, where it says that Christ is King, when the Church speaks to him. In Ecclesiasticus: that the greatness of God cannot be numbered. From this it is taught that those are blasphemers who believe the Trinity should be urged upon [people] by separating it, and by grades and numbers. In Psalm 117, likewise of Wisdom, which is the Son of God, [that] so also the Holy Spirit knows the counsels of the Father: But who knows your counsel, unless you give Wisdom and send the Spirit from the heights? In the same book, that the Son, through whom all things were made, is almighty: For your almighty hand, it says, which created all things, and the world out of formless matter, was not powerless. In the same book: that the Holy Spirit is also the Son: scattered by the Holy Spirit of your power, having suffered persecution from their own deeds. In the same book, of the Holy Spirit, that he is incorruptible: For your incorruptible Spirit is in all things. In the same book, where it calls Christ visible according to the form of the lowliness he took on, but according to the form of deity declares him not visible but invisible, saying: Seeing him whom they had once denied, they recognised [him as] the true God. In the same book: that the Son of God is of the substance of the Father: Instead of these you fed your people with the food of angels, and supplied them without toil with bread ready from heaven, holding every delight in itself and the sweetness of every taste; for you were showing your substance and sweetness, which you have in the Son. In the Gospel according to John: that the Holy Spirit is invisible: The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because the world does not see him nor know him; but you know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you. In the Song it says that Christ is King, when the Church speaks: The king has brought me into his chamber; let us exult and rejoice in you. Again: We will make you likenesses of gold with studs of silver, while the king is on his couch. In Ecclesiasticus: that the greatness of God cannot be numbered. From this it is taught how blasphemous against the Trinity of God are those who think it should be urged by separating [it] with grades and numbers: And who has searched out the dominion of his greatness, and who has numbered his greatness? In Psalm 147, likewise, it is said of Wisdom, which is the Son of God, that there is no number to his wisdom: Great is our Lord, and great his power, and of his wisdom there is no number. Maximinus the Arian, being unable to answer these propositions, put it off from day to day. But Cerealis said to the one who was presiding, to whom [the matter] had been assigned: With God's help I have answered the questions he put forward; why does he not answer my propositions? So when the one to whom [the matter] had been assigned summoned the aforementioned Maximinus, he was silent. And [the official] said to Cerealis: Go away to your own church; for Maximinus, summoned by me, would not answer; from this it is understood that he was not able, since he was silent and would not answer your propositions. Now God hears [the case] between you.
